children.text: The Philippines' summer capital, set in the foothills of the Cordilleras at about
above sea level. With its year-round cool climate, pine forests, strawberry farms, night market, and the Panagbenga flower festival in
February
, it's a city loved by travelers escaping the heat and by students on English-study trips.
Baguio is a city built on a plateau about
above sea level, on the southern side of the Cordillera mountain range in northern Luzon. Its average annual temperature of around
, some

cooler than the lowlands, earned it the nickname "Summer Capital of the Philippines." In the early 20th century, the American colonial government developed it as a city to which the summer administration could relocate to escape sweltering Manila, and the downtown park and street grid designed by Chicago urban planner Daniel Burnham still form the city's backbone today.

The city's name is said to come from "bagiw," the Ibaloi word for moss. The land originally belonged to the Ibaloi and Kankanaey indigenous peoples, and Cordillera indigenous culture still runs through the city's markets, crafts, and food today. With the Philippine Military Academy (PMA) and several universities located here, it is also a student city, and among Korean expats it's well known as a destination for English-language study.
Baguio became a chartered city on
September 1, 1909
, and about 368,000 people (2024 census) live within its roughly 57.51 km² area. The city sits at elevations of
, with neighborhoods perched on hill after hill. The magnitude 7.7 Luzon earthquake of
caused heavy damage to the city, and the Panagbenga flower festival was born out of a resolve to rise above that devastation. In
, recognition of its craft traditions such as woodcarving, silversmithing, and traditional weaving made it the Philippines' first UNESCO Creative City (in the field of Crafts and Folk Art).

Cool air drifting through the pine forests, accommodations with fireplaces, markets piled with strawberries and vegetables, and a night market that opens every evening all combine to give an atmosphere rare among Southeast Asian cities. On the other hand, keep in mind that on weekends and holidays Manila residents pour in and traffic congestion gets heavy.

Baguio suits expat families tired of the heat, travelers who enjoy coffee and cafe tours, and backpackers using it as a gateway to Cordillera mountain trips to Sagada, Mount Pulag, Banaue, and beyond.
You can ride a rowboat on the artificial lake right in the middle of downtown. The city-set rate is around
per boat for
30 minutes
, and bike rentals along the lakeside are also popular with families.

blocks.title: Strolling Session Road and cafe hopping

children.text: This is Baguio's main street, lined with old bakeries, cafes, and bookstores. Seeking out local cafes that serve Benguet-grown Arabica coffee is part of the fun. The roughly
1.7km
street got its name in
, when the Philippine Commission held a session in an old building at its far end and began using Baguio as the summer capital. Climb the 104 steps midway along the street to reach Baguio Cathedral.

An observation deck overlooking the old gold and copper mining district, with layer upon layer of ridges stretching toward Itogon. The souvenir shops around it sell woodcarvings and textiles. It's about
4km
northeast of downtown,
15–20 minutes
by jeepney, and admission is about
. The view is best early in the morning, before fog fills the valley.
In the neighboring town just north of Baguio, you can pick your own strawberries right in the fields. The season runs roughly
December–April
, and be sure to try strawberry taho and strawberry ice cream. It's about
6km
from downtown, and in peak season the strawberries you pick yourself cost about
per kg, more than those sold at roadside stalls. See the
La Trinidad Strawberry Farm
entry for details.

A museum showing the works of National Artist Benedicto Cabrera alongside Cordillera indigenous artifacts. Set in the woods along Asin Road, it also lets you stroll through the garden and ponds out back. The four-story building, opened in

, houses the Cordillera Gallery, a contemporary art gallery, and more, and you can take a break at Café Sabel inside. Flash photography, video recording, drones, and tripods are prohibited, and selfie sticks may be used only in the farm and garden areas.
A shop selling Baguio's signature gifts, such as ube (purple yam) jam and peanut brittle. Popular items sell out by the afternoon, so it's best to go in the morning. It's on Gibraltar Road, a
5–10 minute
walk from Mines View Park, and proceeds from the Mountain Maid Training Center, run by the sisters, go toward student scholarships.

blocks.title: Camp John Hay and the Botanical Garden

children.text: Camp John Hay, once a U.S. military rest and recreation base, is a place to unwind with pine-forest trails and restaurants. At nearby Wright Park, you can also go pony riding. The historic area, which brings together the Bell House, the Bell Amphitheater, and the "Cemetery of Negativism," charges about
for admission, and it is also where Japanese General Yamashita surrendered on
September 3, 1945
. The Botanical Garden on Leonard Wood Road (admission about
) has sculptures and huts reflecting indigenous culture, as well as a tunnel about
long dug by the Japanese army during World War II.
A stall market held every night on Harrison Road next to Burnham Park. It buzzes with a mix of secondhand clothing known as "ukay-ukay" and street food.

Victory Liner, JoyBus, and Solid North buses run from Cubao, Pasay, PITX, and elsewhere in Manila almost
24 hours

4–6 hours

Tickets sell out quickly on weekends, holidays, and during Panagbenga, so use the official app or book online.
From Clark International Airport (Pampanga), Genesis (JoyBus) runs direct to the Governor Pack Road terminal in Baguio in about
3–4 hours
, for a fare of about
. There are only around five departures a day from Clark (from
into the evening), so check them against your flight's arrival time.
Public transport fares, including jeepneys and buses, went up as of
September 28, 2026
, so check the latest fares when booking.
The usual route is via NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX, exiting at Rosales or Pozorrubio and then climbing Marcos Highway. It takes about
4–5 hours
. Kennon Road has better scenery but is often closed for rockfalls or repair work, so check whether it's open beforehand.
After heavy rains in
August 2026
, Kennon Road was closed to non-residents from
early August
and reopened on
August 22
; as of
late September
, only light vehicles of 5 tons or less may use it, and some sections are down to a single lane. Heavy vehicles are advised to take Marcos Highway or Asin Road (toward La Union).
Baguio Loakan Airport has had no scheduled passenger flights since the Cebu route was suspended in
July 2024
, so it is not a realistic option. If you are coming from overseas, landing at Clark International Airport (CRK) and going by bus is the closest.

items.title: From La Union and the mountain areas

children.text: Baguio is linked to San Fernando and San Juan in La Union by Naguilian Road; buses and vans from the terminals near Governor Pack Road take about
1.5–2 hours
, with fares of about

Buses and vans to mountain areas such as Sagada, Atok, and Kabayan leave from around the Dangwa Terminal and the Slaughterhouse Terminal and climb the Halsema Highway. Most departures are bunched in the early morning, so check departure times the day before.
Downtown has many white taxis with a cheap flag-down rate, convenient for short trips. Even for a short distance, always ask the driver to turn on the meter.
Jeepney stops for each route are clustered below Session Road and around the market, and a ride costs about
. Because it is highland, there are almost no tricycles.
From
September 28, 2026
, the minimum fare is
for traditional jeepneys and
for modern jeepneys (for the first
4km
). Students, seniors, and persons with disabilities get a 20% discount.
Downtown may enforce vehicle restrictions based on the last digit of the license plate (number coding), so check the latest rules before driving a private car.
Baguio is cool all year, but the seasons still differ clearly.
November–February
is the coolest stretch, with dawn temperatures dropping to around
, and the atmosphere is especially good with Christmas lights overlapping the strawberry season. In
February
, the city's biggest event, the Panagbenga flower festival, runs for nearly a month; in
, the street dance parade in
late February
and the flower float parade in
early March
were the highlights. Accommodation prices rise and downtown traffic is restricted on festival weekends.
March–April
is clear and mild, making it the peak season with the most tourists, and the city gets extremely crowded during Holy Week in particular. Afternoon showers become frequent from
May
, and
June–October

is the rainy season; Baguio is one of the rainiest cities in the Philippines. When a typhoon passes, several hundred mm of rain can fall in a single day, thick fog sets in, and landslides on mountain roads can block traffic, so check the weather forecast carefully during this period.
According to PAGASA (the Philippine weather bureau) climate normals, January averages a low of
and a high of
with just over three rainy days, but of the roughly 3,800mm of annual rainfall, about 960mm falls in August alone. The lowest temperature on record is
, on
January 18, 1961
. Panagbenga celebrated its 30th edition in
; after the parades, Session Road became a car-free flower street (Session Road in Bloom) from
March 2–8
, and the festival closed with fireworks on
March 8
. The schedule changes every year, so check Baguio City announcements.

and may vary depending on local conditions.

For a first visit, the area around Session Road and Burnham Park is the most convenient — you can walk to the market, night market, and restaurants, and it's also close to the bus terminals. If you want a quiet, pleasant place to stay, choose a pine-forest hotel around Camp John Hay or a boutique hotel around Legarda Road or Asin Road. Prices run about
per night for a guesthouse and about
for a mid-range hotel, and can nearly double during Panagbenga and Holy Week. Baguio accommodations often skip air conditioning but come standard with hot water and thick blankets.

True to a "highland city," the food here centers on fresh vegetables, strawberries, and coffee. Signature dishes include salads and soups made with Benguet vegetables, the Cordillera smoked-pork dish "etag," strawberry taho, and ube jam, and Session Road and the area near Burnham Park have many bakeries and cafes that have been running for decades. The cheap eateries (carinderias) on the second floor of the public market are great if you want to eat like a local. On cold nights, the hot soup dish "bulalo" (beef bone-marrow soup) is a perfect match.

Long-loved restaurants include Good Taste on Otek Street, open 24 hours (butter chicken and fried rice); Café by the Ruins on Shuntug Road (sweet potato bread and Baguio longganisa breakfasts); Oh My Gulay, a vegetarian restaurant on the 5th floor of the La Azotea Building on Session Road; and Vizco's, famous for its strawberry shortcake. Typical souvenirs are strawberry jam, peanuts, brooms, and woodcarvings from the public market, which is generally cheaper than the stalls at Mines View.
Bring long sleeves and a light padded jacket or windbreaker. Even if short sleeves are fine during the day, it turns quite cold at night and dawn.
From Friday evening to Sunday afternoon on weekends, traffic around Marcos Highway and Session Road gets very heavy. Visit on weekdays if you can.
The night market usually runs from around
9 PM
until dawn. It gets crowded, so wear your bag on your front and carry only small amounts of cash.
Downtown is full of slopes, so comfortable walking shoes are essential.
Go to the Good Shepherd souvenir shop and the strawberry farms early in the morning to avoid sellouts and crowds.
Downtown has plenty of ATMs and convenience stores, so cash isn't much of a worry, but if you plan to continue on to mountain areas like Sagada or Mount Pulag, withdraw enough cash in Baguio first.
Most of the city is a no-smoking zone, and smoking outside designated areas can be fined.
The BenCab Museum is closed on Mondays, Christmas, and New Year's Day, and open Tuesday to Sunday from
9 AM to 6 PM

The Mansion reopened as a presidential museum on
September 8, 2024

9 AM to 6 PM
. Book guided tours in advance; walk-ins can join if there's space (

The city council is discussing an environmental fee for tourists (aiming for passage in
); if it takes effect, you may need to register your visit and pay the fee. Check Baguio City announcements before you go.
During the rainy season (
June–October
) and after typhoons, Kennon Road and other mountain roads are often closed due to landslides. Be sure to check road conditions and the PAGASA forecast before you set out. In
August 2026
, heavy rain from Tropical Storm Maymay and the southwest monsoon triggered more than 20 landslides in the city, and there were fatalities.
Driving mountain roads at night in thick fog is very dangerous. If it's your first time, travel during daylight hours.
Baguio has fairly strict ordinances on smoking, single-use plastics, and noise. Follow the local rules.
At about
above sea level, you may feel a mild headache or shortness of breath. Don't push yourself on the first day, and drink plenty of water.
Watch out for pickpockets at the night market and public market, and don't keep your phone in your back pocket.
If a taxi driver asks for a flat fare instead of using the meter, it's better to take a different taxi.
